}## Expand description

Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

The `Arbitrary` trait allows you to generate valid structured values, like
`HashMap`s, or ASTs, or `MyTomlConfig`, or any other data structure from
raw, unstructured bytes provided by a fuzzer.

[§](https://docs.rs#deriving-arbitrary)Deriving `Arbitrary`

Automatically deriving the `Arbitrary` trait is the recommended way to
implement `Arbitrary` for your types.

Using the custom derive requires that you enable the `"derive"` cargo
feature in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
arbitrary = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
```
Then, you add the `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` annotation to your `struct` or
`enum` type definition:

```
use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
use std::collections::HashSet;
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
pub struct AddressBook {
    friends: HashSet<Friend>,
}
#[derive(Arbitrary, Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub enum Friend {
    Buddy { name: String },
    Pal { age: usize },
}
```
Every member of the `struct` or `enum` must also implement `Arbitrary`.

It is also possible to change the default bounds added by the derive:

```
use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
trait Trait {
    type Assoc: for<'a> Arbitrary<'a>;
}
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
// The bounds are used verbatim, so any existing trait bounds will need to be repeated.
#[arbitrary(bound = "T: Trait")]
struct Point<T: Trait> {
    x: T::Assoc,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-arbitrary-by-hand)Implementing `Arbitrary` By Hand

Implementing `Arbitrary` mostly involves nested calls to other `Arbitrary`
arbitrary implementations for each of your `struct` or `enum`’s members. But
sometimes you need some amount of raw data, or you need to generate a
variably-sized collection type, or something of that sort. The
[ Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html) type helps you with these tasks.

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
impl<'a, T> Arbitrary<'a> for MyCollection<T>
where
    T: Arbitrary<'a>,
{
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
        // Get an iterator of arbitrary `T`s.
        let iter = u.arbitrary_iter::<T>()?;
        // And then create a collection!
        let mut my_collection = MyCollection::new();
        for elem_result in iter {
            let elem = elem_result?;
            my_collection.insert(elem);
        }
        Ok(my_collection)
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#a-note-on-output-distributions)A Note On Output Distributions

There is no requirement for a particular distribution of the values. For
example, it is not required that every value appears with the same
probability. That being said, the main use for `Arbitrary` is for fuzzing,
so in many cases a uniform distribution will make the most sense in order to
provide the best coverage of the domain. In other cases this is not
desirable or even possible, for example when sampling from a uniform
distribution is computationally expensive or in the case of collections that
may grow indefinitely.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#207)#### fn [arbitrary](https://docs.rs#tymethod.arbitrary)(u: &mut [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#207)

#### fn [arbitrary](https://docs.rs#tymethod.arbitrary)(u: &mut [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

Generate an arbitrary value of `Self` from the given unstructured data.

Calling `Arbitrary::arbitrary` requires that you have some raw data,
perhaps given to you by a fuzzer like AFL or libFuzzer. You wrap this
raw data in an `Unstructured`, and then you can call `<MyType as Arbitrary>::arbitrary` to construct an arbitrary instance of `MyType`
from that unstructured data.

Implementations may return an error if there is not enough data to
construct a full instance of `Self`, or they may fill out the rest of
`Self` with dummy values. Using dummy values when the underlying data is
exhausted can help avoid accidentally “defeating” some of the fuzzer’s
mutations to the underlying byte stream that might otherwise lead to
interesting runtime behavior or new code coverage if only we had just a
few more bytes. However, it also requires that implementations for
recursive types (e.g. `struct Foo(Option<Box<Foo>>)`) avoid infinite
recursion when the underlying data is exhausted.

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Unstructured};
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
pub struct MyType {
    // ...
}
// Get the raw data from the fuzzer or wherever else.
let raw_data: &[u8] = get_raw_data_from_fuzzer();
// Wrap that raw data in an `Unstructured`.
let mut unstructured = Unstructured::new(raw_data);
// Generate an arbitrary instance of `MyType` and do stuff with it.
if let Ok(value) = MyType::arbitrary(&mut unstructured) {
    do_stuff(value);
}
```
See also the documentation for [ Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html).

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#216-218)#### fn [arbitrary_take_rest](https://docs.rs#method.arbitrary_take_rest)(u: [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#216-218)

#### fn [arbitrary_take_rest](https://docs.rs#method.arbitrary_take_rest)(u: [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

Generate an arbitrary value of `Self` from the entirety of the given
unstructured data.

This is similar to Arbitrary::arbitrary, however it assumes that it is
the last consumer of the given data, and is thus able to consume it all
if it needs.  See also the documentation for
[ Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html).

Get a size hint for how many bytes out of an `Unstructured` this type
needs to construct itself.

This is useful for determining how many elements we should insert when creating an arbitrary collection.

The return value is similar to [ Iterator::size_hint](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.size_hint): it returns a
tuple where the first element is a lower bound on the number of bytes
required, and the second element is an optional upper bound.

The default implementation return `(0, None)` which is correct for any
type, but not ultimately that useful. Using `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` will
create a better implementation. If you are writing an `Arbitrary`
implementation by hand, and your type can be part of a dynamically sized
collection (such as `Vec`), you are strongly encouraged to override this
default with a better implementation, and also override
[ try_size_hint](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.try_size_hint).

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-implement-this)How to implement this

If the size hint calculation is a trivial constant and does not recurse
into any other `size_hint` call, you should implement it in `size_hint`:

```
use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
struct SomeStruct(u8);
impl<'a> Arbitrary<'a> for SomeStruct {
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
        let buf = &mut [0];
        u.fill_buffer(buf)?;
        Ok(SomeStruct(buf[0]))
    }
    #[inline]
    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        let _ = depth;
        (1, Some(1))
    }
}
```
Otherwise, it should instead be implemented in [ try_size_hint](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.try_size_hint),
and the

`size_hint` implementation should forward to it:```
use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, MaxRecursionReached, Result, Unstructured};
struct SomeStruct<A, B> {
    a: A,
    b: B,
}
impl<'a, A: Arbitrary<'a>, B: Arbitrary<'a>> Arbitrary<'a> for SomeStruct<A, B> {
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
        // ...
    }
    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        // Return the value of try_size_hint
        //
        // If the recursion fails, return the default, always valid `(0, None)`
        Self::try_size_hint(depth).unwrap_or_default()
    }
    fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
        // Protect against potential infinite recursion with
        // `try_recursion_guard`.
        size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth, |depth| {
            // If we aren't too deep, then `recursion_guard` calls
            // this closure, which implements the natural size hint.
            // Don't forget to use the new `depth` in all nested
            // `try_size_hint` calls! We recommend shadowing the
            // parameter, like what is done here, so that you can't
            // accidentally use the wrong depth.
            Ok(size_hint::and(
                <A as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
                <B as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
            ))
        })
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#invariant)Invariant

It must be possible to construct every possible output using only inputs
of lengths bounded by these parameters. This applies to both
[ Arbitrary::arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#tymethod.arbitrary) and

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.arbitrary_take_rest)

`Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest`This is trivially true for `(0, None)`. To restrict this further, it
must be proven that all inputs that are now excluded produced redundant
outputs which are still possible to produce using the reduced input
space.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#423-425)#### fn [try_size_hint](https://docs.rs#method.try_size_hint)(
    depth: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>), [MaxRecursionReached](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#423-425)

#### fn [try_size_hint](https://docs.rs#method.try_size_hint)(
    depth: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>), [MaxRecursionReached](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)>

Get a size hint for how many bytes out of an `Unstructured` this type
needs to construct itself.

Unlike [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html), this function keeps the information that the
recursion limit was reached. This is required to “short circuit” the
calculation and avoid exponential blowup with recursive structures.

If you are implementing [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html) for a struct that could be
recursive, you should implement

`try_size_hint` and call the
`try_size_hint` when recursingThe return value is similar to [ core::iter::Iterator::size_hint](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.size_hint): it
returns a tuple where the first element is a lower bound on the number
of bytes required, and the second element is an optional upper bound.

The default implementation returns the value of [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html) which is
correct for any type, but might lead to exponential blowup when dealing
with recursive types.

[§](https://docs.rs#invariant-1)Invariant

It must be possible to construct every possible output using only inputs
of lengths bounded by these parameters. This applies to both
[ Arbitrary::arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#tymethod.arbitrary) and

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.arbitrary_take_rest)

`Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest`This is trivially true for `(0, None)`. To restrict this further, it
must be proven that all inputs that are now excluded produced redundant
outputs which are still possible to produce using the reduced input
space.

[§](https://docs.rs#when-to-implement-try_size_hint)When to implement `try_size_hint`

If you 100% know that the type you are implementing `Arbitrary` for is
not a recursive type, or your implementation is not transitively calling
any other `size_hint` methods, you may implement [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html), and the
default

`try_size_hint` implementation will use it.Note that if you are implementing `Arbitrary` for a generic type, you
cannot guarantee the lack of type recursion!

Otherwise, when there is possible type recursion, you should implement
`try_size_hint` instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-depth-parameter)The `depth` parameter

When implementing `try_size_hint`, you need to use
[ arbitrary::size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth)](https://docs.rs/size_hint/fn.try_recursion_guard.html)
to prevent potential infinite recursion when calculating size hints for
potentially recursive types:

```
use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, MaxRecursionReached, Unstructured};
// This can potentially be a recursive type if `L` or `R` contain
// something like `Box<Option<MyEither<L, R>>>`!
enum MyEither<L, R> {
    Left(L),
    Right(R),
}
impl<'a, L, R> Arbitrary<'a> for MyEither<L, R>
where
    L: Arbitrary<'a>,
    R: Arbitrary<'a>,
{
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured) -> arbitrary::Result<Self> {
        // ...
    }
    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        // Return the value of `try_size_hint`
        //
        // If the recursion fails, return the default `(0, None)` range,
        // which is always valid.
        Self::try_size_hint(depth).unwrap_or_default()
    }
    fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
        // Protect against potential infinite recursion with
        // `try_recursion_guard`.
        size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth, |depth| {
            // If we aren't too deep, then `recursion_guard` calls
            // this closure, which implements the natural size hint.
            // Don't forget to use the new `depth` in all nested
            // `try_size_hint` calls! We recommend shadowing the
            // parameter, like what is done here, so that you can't
            // accidentally use the wrong depth.
            Ok(size_hint::or(
                <L as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
                <R as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
            ))
        })
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arbitrary/latest/arbitrary/

## Expand description

The `Arbitrary` trait crate.

This trait provides an [ Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html) trait to
produce well-typed, structured values, from raw, byte buffers. It is
generally intended to be used with fuzzers like AFL or libFuzzer. See the

[trait’s documentation for details on automatically deriving, implementing, and/or using the trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`Arbitrary`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [size_](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html)- hint
- Utilities for working with and combining the results of
`Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [unstructured](https://docs.rs/unstructured/index.html)
- Wrappers around raw, unstructured bytes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [MaxRecursion](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)- Reached
- Error indicating that the maximum recursion depth has been reached while calculating `Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)
- A source of unstructured data.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An enumeration of buffer creation errors

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A `Result`with the error type fixed as`arbitrary::Error`.

# serde_big_array - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde-big-array/latest/serde_big_array/

## Expand description

Big array helper for serde.
The purpose of this crate is to make (de-)serializing arrays of sizes > 32 easy.
This solution is needed until [serde adopts const generics support](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde/issues/1937).

This crates provides you with two tools to use big arrays in your crate:

- The first tool is the `BigArray``serde_derive`macro and an`#[serde(with = "BigArray")]`next to your data declaration.
- The second tool is the `Array``BigArray`

We recommended using the [ BigArray](https://docs.rs/trait.BigArray.html) trait in most cases, and using the

[struct only if](https://docs.rs/struct.Array.html)

`Array`[doesn’t work.](https://docs.rs/trait.BigArray.html)

`BigArray`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
extern crate serde;
#[macro_use]
extern crate serde_derive;
extern crate serde_json;
extern crate serde_big_array;
use serde_big_array::BigArray;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct S {
    #[serde(with = "BigArray")]
    arr: [u8; 64],
}
#[test]
fn test() {
    let s = S { arr: [1; 64] };
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&s).unwrap();
    let s_back = serde_json::from_str::<S>(&j).unwrap();
    assert!(&s.arr[..] == &s_back.arr[..]);
    assert!(false);
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Array](https://docs.rs/struct.Array.html)
- An array newtype usable for nested structures

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BigArray](https://docs.rs/trait.BigArray.html)
- The big array serialization helper trait

# borsh - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/borsh/latest/borsh/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

[§](https://docs.rs#ecosystem-features)Ecosystem features

-
**std**- When enabled,`borsh`uses the standard library. Disabling this feature will result in building the crate in`no_std`environment.To carter such builds, Borsh offers `io``BorshSerialize``BorshDeserialize``io::Read`,`io::Write`and`io::Result`.When **std**feature is enabled, those items are re-exports of corresponding`std::io`items. Otherwise they are borsh-specific types which mimic behaviour of corresponding standard types.

[§](https://docs.rs#default-features)Default features

- **std**- enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-features)Other features

-
**derive**- Gates derive macros of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)traits.
-
**unstable__schema**- Gates[BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)trait and its derive macro. Gates[schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)module. This feature requires**derive**to be enabled too.
-
**rc**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for`Rc<T>``Arc<T>``no_std`setting`Rc`/`Arc`are pulled from`alloc`crate. Serializing and deserializing these types does not preserve identity and may result in multiple copies of the same data. Be sure that this is what you want before enabling this feature.
-
**hashbrown**- Pulls in[HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/[HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html)when no`std`is available. This feature is set to be mutually exclusive with**std**feature.
-
**bytes**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[Bytes](https://docs.rs/bytes/1.5.0/bytes/struct.Bytes.html)and[BytesMut](https://docs.rs/bytes/1.5.0/bytes/struct.BytesMut.html). In`no_std`builds this keeps`bytes`in`no_std`mode; when**std**is enabled,`bytes/std`is enabled as well.
-
**bson**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[ObjectId](https://docs.rs/bson/2.9.0/bson/oid/struct.ObjectId.html).
-
**indexmap**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[indexmap::IndexMap](https://docs.rs/indexmap/2.8.0/indexmap/map/struct.IndexMap.html)and[IndexSet](https://docs.rs/indexmap/2.8.0/indexmap/set/struct.IndexSet.html)
-
**ascii**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html),[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html),[BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)for types from[ascii](https://docs.rs/ascii/1.1.0/ascii/)crate.
-
**de_strict_order**- Enables check that keys, parsed during deserialization of[HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/[HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html)and[BTreeSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/set/struct.BTreeSet.html)/[BTreeMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/map/struct.BTreeMap.html)are encountered in ascending order with respect to[PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html)for hash collections, and[Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html)for btree ones. Deserialization emits error otherwise.If this feature is not enabled, it is possible that two different byte slices could deserialize into the same `HashMap`/`HashSet`object.

[§](https://docs.rs#config-aliases)Config aliases

- **hash_collections**- This is a feature alias, set up in- `build.rs`to be equivalent to (- **std**OR- **hashbrown**). Gates implementation of- [BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html),- [BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)and- [BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)for- [HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/- [HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#shortcuts)Shortcuts

# AsPrimitive in num_traits::cast - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-traits/latest/num_traits/cast/trait.AsPrimitive.html

## Expand description

A generic interface for casting between machine scalars with the
`as` operator, which admits narrowing and precision loss.
Implementers of this trait `AsPrimitive` should behave like a primitive
numeric type (e.g. a newtype around another primitive), and the
intended conversion must never fail.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let three: i32 = (3.14159265f32).as_();
assert_eq!(three, 3);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

**In Rust versions before 1.45.0**, some uses of the `as` operator were not entirely safe.
In particular, it was undefined behavior if
a truncated floating point value could not fit in the target integer
type ([#10184](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/10184)).

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_integer/lib.rs.html#159-192)

#### fn [extended_gcd](https://docs.rs#method.extended_gcd)(&self, other: &Self) -> [ExtendedGcd](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtendedGcd.html)<Self>

Greatest common divisor and Bézout coefficients.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
fn check<A: Copy + Integer + NumAssign>(a: A, b: A) -> bool {
    let ExtendedGcd { gcd, x, y, .. } = a.extended_gcd(&b);
    gcd == x * a + y * b
}
assert!(check(10isize, 4isize));
assert!(check(8isize,  9isize));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_integer/lib.rs.html#279-281)#### fn [div_mod_floor](https://docs.rs#method.div_mod_floor)(&self, other: &Self) -> (Self, Self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_integer/lib.rs.html#279-281)

#### fn [div_mod_floor](https://docs.rs#method.div_mod_floor)(&self, other: &Self) -> (Self, Self)

Simultaneous floored integer division and modulus.
Returns `(quotient, remainder)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
assert_eq!(( 8).div_mod_floor( &3), ( 2,  2));
assert_eq!(( 8).div_mod_floor(&-3), (-3, -1));
assert_eq!((-8).div_mod_floor( &3), (-3,  1));
assert_eq!((-8).div_mod_floor(&-3), ( 2, -2));
assert_eq!(( 1).div_mod_floor( &2), ( 0,  1));
assert_eq!(( 1).div_mod_floor(&-2), (-1, -1));
assert_eq!((-1).div_mod_floor( &2), (-1,  1));
assert_eq!((-1).div_mod_floor(&-2), ( 0, -1));
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_integer/lib.rs.html#303-314)#### fn [next_multiple_of](https://docs.rs#method.next_multiple_of)(&self, other: &Self) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_integer/lib.rs.html#303-314)

#### fn [next_multiple_of](https://docs.rs#method.next_multiple_of)(&self, other: &Self) -> Self

Rounds up to nearest multiple of argument.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

For signed types, `a.next_multiple_of(b) = a.prev_multiple_of(b.neg())`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
assert_eq!(( 16).next_multiple_of(& 8),  16);
assert_eq!(( 23).next_multiple_of(& 8),  24);
assert_eq!(( 16).next_multiple_of(&-8),  16);
assert_eq!(( 23).next_multiple_of(&-8),  16);
assert_eq!((-16).next_multiple_of(& 8), -16);
assert_eq!((-23).next_multiple_of(& 8), -16);
assert_eq!((-16).next_multiple_of(&-8), -16);
assert_eq!((-23).next_multiple_of(&-8), -24);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_integer/lib.rs.html#336-341)#### fn [prev_multiple_of](https://docs.rs#method.prev_multiple_of)(&self, other: &Self) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_integer/lib.rs.html#336-341)

#### fn [prev_multiple_of](https://docs.rs#method.prev_multiple_of)(&self, other: &Self) -> Self

Rounds down to nearest multiple of argument.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes-1)Notes

For signed types, `a.prev_multiple_of(b) = a.next_multiple_of(b.neg())`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
assert_eq!(( 16).prev_multiple_of(& 8),  16);
assert_eq!(( 23).prev_multiple_of(& 8),  16);
assert_eq!(( 16).prev_multiple_of(&-8),  16);
assert_eq!(( 23).prev_multiple_of(&-8),  24);
assert_eq!((-16).prev_multiple_of(& 8), -16);
assert_eq!((-23).prev_multiple_of(& 8), -24);
assert_eq!((-16).prev_multiple_of(&-8), -16);
assert_eq!((-23).prev_multiple_of(&-8), -16);
```

# Roots in num_integer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-integer/latest/num_integer/trait.Roots.html

`pub trait Roots: `[Integer](https://docs.rs/trait.Integer.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [nth_root](https://docs.rs#tymethod.nth_root)(&self, n: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> Self;
    // Provided methods
    fn [sqrt](https://docs.rs#method.sqrt)(&self) -> Self { ... }
[cbrt](https://docs.rs#method.cbrt)(&self) -> Self { ... }
}## Expand description

Provides methods to compute an integer’s square root, cube root,
and arbitrary `n`th root.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Returns the truncated principal `n`th root of an integer
– `if x >= 0 { ⌊ⁿ√x⌋ } else { ⌈ⁿ√x⌉ }`

This is solving for `r` in `rⁿ = x`, rounding toward zero.
If `x` is positive, the result will satisfy `rⁿ ≤ x < (r+1)ⁿ`.
If `x` is negative and `n` is odd, then `(r-1)ⁿ < x ≤ rⁿ`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if `n` is zero:

or if `n` is even and `self` is negative:

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use num_integer::Roots;
let x: i32 = 12345;
assert_eq!(x.nth_root(1), x);
assert_eq!(x.nth_root(2), x.sqrt());
assert_eq!(x.nth_root(3), x.cbrt());
assert_eq!(x.nth_root(4), 10);
assert_eq!(x.nth_root(13), 2);
assert_eq!(x.nth_root(14), 1);
assert_eq!(x.nth_root(std::u32::MAX), 1);
assert_eq!(std::i32::MAX.nth_root(30), 2);
assert_eq!(std::i32::MAX.nth_root(31), 1);
assert_eq!(std::i32::MIN.nth_root(31), -2);
assert_eq!((std::i32::MIN + 1).nth_root(31), -1);
assert_eq!(std::u32::MAX.nth_root(31), 2);
assert_eq!(std::u32::MAX.nth_root(32), 1);
```
## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Returns the truncated principal square root of an integer – `⌊√x⌋`

This is solving for `r` in `r² = x`, rounding toward zero.
The result will satisfy `r² ≤ x < (r+1)²`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

Panics if `self` is less than zero:

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use num_integer::Roots;
let x: i32 = 12345;
assert_eq!((x * x).sqrt(), x);
assert_eq!((x * x + 1).sqrt(), x);
assert_eq!((x * x - 1).sqrt(), x - 1);
```
Returns the truncated principal cube root of an integer –
`if x >= 0 { ⌊∛x⌋ } else { ⌈∛x⌉ }`

This is solving for `r` in `r³ = x`, rounding toward zero.
If `x` is positive, the result will satisfy `r³ ≤ x < (r+1)³`.
If `x` is negative, then `(r-1)³ < x ≤ r³`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use num_integer::Roots;
let x: i32 = 1234;
assert_eq!((x * x * x).cbrt(), x);
assert_eq!((x * x * x + 1).cbrt(), x);
assert_eq!((x * x * x - 1).cbrt(), x - 1);
assert_eq!((-(x * x * x)).cbrt(), -x);
assert_eq!((-(x * x * x + 1)).cbrt(), -x);
assert_eq!((-(x * x * x - 1)).cbrt(), -(x - 1));
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Arbitrary in quickcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quickcheck/latest/quickcheck/trait.Arbitrary.html

`pub trait Arbitrary: `[Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + 'static {
    // Required method
    fn [arbitrary](https://docs.rs#tymethod.arbitrary)(g: &mut [Gen](https://docs.rs/struct.Gen.html)) -> Self;
    // Provided method
    fn [shrink](https://docs.rs#method.shrink)(&self) -> [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html)<Item = Self>> { ... }
}## Expand description

`Arbitrary` describes types whose values can be randomly generated and
shrunk.

Aside from shrinking, `Arbitrary` is different from typical RNGs in that it
respects `Gen::size()` for controlling how much memory a particular value
uses, for practical purposes. For example, `Vec::arbitrary()` respects
`Gen::size()` to decide the maximum `len()` of the vector. This behavior is
necessary due to practical speed and size limitations. Conversely,
`i32::arbitrary()` ignores `size()` since all `i32` values require `O(1)`
memory and operations between `i32`s require `O(1)` time (with the
exception of exponentiation).

Additionally, all types that implement `Arbitrary` must also implement
`Clone`.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Return an arbitrary value.

Implementations should respect `Gen::size()` when decisions about how
big a particular value should be. Implementations should generally
defer to other `Arbitrary` implementations to generate other random
values when necessary. The `Gen` type also offers a few RNG helper
routines.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Return an iterator of values that are smaller than itself.

The way in which a value is “smaller” is implementation defined. In
some cases, the interpretation is obvious: shrinking an integer should
produce integers smaller than itself. Others are more complex, for
example, shrinking a `Vec` should both shrink its size and shrink its
component values.

The iterator returned should be bounded to some reasonable size.

It is always correct to return an empty iterator, and indeed, this is the default implementation. The downside of this approach is that witnesses to failures in properties will be more inscrutable.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# quickcheck - Rust

## Expand description

This crate is a port of
[Haskell’s QuickCheck](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/QuickCheck).

QuickCheck is a library for random testing of program properties. The programmer provides a specification of the program, in the form of properties which functions should satisfy, and QuickCheck then tests that the properties hold in a large number of randomly generated cases.

For detailed examples, please see the
[README](https://github.com/BurntSushi/quickcheck).

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

In general, this crate considers the `Arbitrary` implementations provided as
implementation details. Strategies may or may not change over time, which may
cause new test failures, presumably due to the discovery of new bugs due to a
new kind of witness being generated. These sorts of changes may happen in
semver compatible releases.

# zeroize - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/zeroize/latest/zeroize/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rustcrypto-zeroize)[RustCrypto](https://github.com/RustCrypto): zeroize

Securely zero memory (a.k.a. [zeroize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeroisation)) while avoiding compiler optimizations.

This crate implements a portable approach to securely zeroing memory using techniques which guarantee they won’t be “optimized away” by the compiler.

The [ Zeroize trait](https://docs.rs/zeroize/latest/zeroize/trait.Zeroize.html) is the crate’s primary API.

[§](https://docs.rs#about)About

[Zeroing memory securely is hard](http://www.daemonology.net/blog/2014-09-04-how-to-zero-a-buffer.html) - compilers optimize for performance, and
in doing so they love to “optimize away” unnecessary zeroing calls. There are
many documented “tricks” to attempt to avoid these optimizations and ensure
that a zeroing routine is performed reliably.

This crate isn’t about tricks: it uses [core::ptr::write_volatile](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/ptr/fn.write_volatile.html)
and [core::sync::atomic](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/core/sync/atomic/index.html) memory fences to provide easy-to-use, portable
zeroing behavior which works on all of Rust’s core number types and slices
thereof, implemented in pure Rust with no usage of FFI or assembly.

- No insecure fallbacks!
- No dependencies!
- No FFI or inline assembly! **WASM friendly**(and tested)!
- `#![no_std]`i.e.- **embedded-friendly**!
- No functionality besides securely zeroing memory!
- (Optional) Custom derive support for zeroing complex structures

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

Requires Rust **1.85** or newer.

In the future, we reserve the right to change MSRV (i.e. MSRV is out-of-scope for this crate’s semantic versioning guarantees).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use zeroize::Zeroize;
// Protip: don't embed secrets in your source code.
// This is just an example.
let mut secret = b"Air shield password: 1,2,3,4,5".to_vec();
// [ ... ] open the air shield here
// Now that we're done using the secret, zero it out.
secret.zeroize();
```

may-or-may-not contain secrets, for example the

`Zeroize`[§](https://docs.rs#custom-derive-support)Custom Derive Support

This crate has custom derive support for the `Zeroize` trait,
gated under the `zeroize` crate’s `zeroize_derive` Cargo feature,
which automatically calls `zeroize()` on all members of a struct
or tuple struct.

Attributes supported for `Zeroize`:

On the item level:

- `#[zeroize(drop)]`:- *deprecated*use- `ZeroizeOnDrop`instead
- `#[zeroize(bound = "T: MyTrait")]`: this replaces any trait bounds inferred by zeroize

On the field level:

- `#[zeroize(skip)]`: skips this field or variant when calling- `zeroize()`

Attributes supported for `ZeroizeOnDrop`:

On the field level:

- `#[zeroize(skip)]`: skips this field or variant when calling- `zeroize()`

Example which derives `Drop`:

```
use zeroize::{Zeroize, ZeroizeOnDrop};
// This struct will be zeroized on drop
#[derive(Zeroize, ZeroizeOnDrop)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
Example which does not derive `Drop` (useful for e.g. `Copy` types)

```
#[cfg(feature = "zeroize_derive")]
use zeroize::Zeroize;
// This struct will *NOT* be zeroized on drop
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Zeroize)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
Example which only derives `Drop`:

```
use zeroize::ZeroizeOnDrop;
// This struct will be zeroized on drop
#[derive(ZeroizeOnDrop)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#zeroizingz-wrapper-for-zeroizing-arbitrary-values-on-drop)`Zeroizing<Z>`: wrapper for zeroizing arbitrary values on drop

`Zeroizing<Z: Zeroize>` is a generic wrapper type that impls `Deref`
and `DerefMut`, allowing access to an inner value of type `Z`, and also
impls a `Drop` handler which calls `zeroize()` on its contents:

```
use zeroize::Zeroizing;
fn use_secret() {
    let mut secret = Zeroizing::new([0u8; 5]);
    // Set the air shield password
    // Protip (again): don't embed secrets in your source code.
    secret.copy_from_slice(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
    assert_eq!(secret.as_ref(), &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
    // The contents of `secret` will be automatically zeroized on drop
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#what-guarantees-does-this-crate-provide)What guarantees does this crate provide?

This crate guarantees the zeroing operation can’t be “optimized away” by the compiler, as ensured by LLVM’s volatile semantics.

Previously there were worries that the approach used by this crate (mixing volatile and
non-volatile accesses) was undefined behavior due to language contained
in the documentation for `write_volatile`, however after some discussion
within the [Unsafe Code Guidelines Working Group](https://github.com/rust-lang/unsafe-code-guidelines), [these remarks have been removed](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/60972) and the
specific usage pattern in this crate is considered to be well-defined.

All of that said, there is still potential for microarchitectural attacks (ala Spectre/Meltdown) to leak “zeroized” secrets through covert channels. This crate makes no guarantees that zeroized values cannot be leaked through such channels, as they represent flaws in the underlying hardware.

[§](https://docs.rs#stackheap-zeroing-notes)Stack/Heap Zeroing Notes

This crate can be used to zero values from either the stack or the heap. We recommend storing sensitive data on the heap whenever possible to reduce the potential for making copies in memory via Rust move semantics, however note that stack spilling and other optimizations may leave temporary copies of data from the heap on the stack.

[ zeroize_stack](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroize_stack.html) can be used to zeroize stack memory.

[ Pin](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/pin/struct.Pin.html) can be leveraged in conjunction with this crate to ensure data kept
on the stack isn’t moved.

The `Zeroize` impls for `Vec`, `String` and `CString` zeroize the entire capacity of their
backing buffer, but cannot guarantee copies of the data were not previously made by buffer
reallocation. It’s therefore important when attempting to zeroize such buffers to initialize
them to the correct capacity, and take care to prevent subsequent reallocation.

The [ secrecy](https://docs.rs/secrecy) crate provides higher-level abstractions for eliminating
usage patterns which can cause reallocations:

[§](https://docs.rs#what-about-clearing-registers-mlock-mprotect-etc)What about: clearing registers, `mlock()`, `mprotect()`, etc?

This crate is focused on providing simple, unobtrusive support for reliably zeroing memory using the best approach possible on stable Rust.

Clearing registers is a difficult problem that can’t easily be solved by
something like a crate, and requires either inline ASM or rustc support.
See [https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/17046](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/17046) for background on
this particular problem.

Other memory protection mechanisms are interesting and useful, but often overkill (e.g. defending against RAM scraping or attackers with swap access). In as much as there may be merit to these approaches, there are also many other crates that already implement more sophisticated memory protections. Such protections are explicitly out-of-scope for this crate.

Zeroing memory is [good cryptographic hygiene](https://github.com/veorq/cryptocoding#clean-memory-of-secret-data) and this crate seeks to promote
it in the most unobtrusive manner possible. This includes omitting complex
`unsafe` memory protection systems and just trying to make the best memory
zeroing crate available.

dynamically sized values or trait objects. It would be inefficient to use this function on a
type that already implements `ZeroizeOnDrop`.
- [zeroize_](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroize_stack.html)- stack
- Zeroize `N`bytes of stack space.

# valuable - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/valuable/latest/valuable/

## Expand description

Valuable provides object-safe value inspection. Use cases include passing structured data to trait objects and object-safe serialization.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

First, derive [ Valuable](https://docs.rs/derive.Valuable.html) on your types.

```
use valuable::Valuable;
#[derive(Valuable)]
struct HelloWorld {
    message: Message,
}
#[derive(Valuable)]
enum Message {
    HelloWorld,
    Custom(String),
}
```
Then, implement a [visitor](https://docs.rs/trait.Visit.html) to inspect the data.

```
use valuable::{NamedValues, Value, Valuable, Visit};
struct Print;
impl Visit for Print {
    fn visit_value(&mut self, value: Value<'_>) {
        match value {
            Value::Structable(v) => {
                println!("struct {}", v.definition().name());
                v.visit(self);
            }
            Value::Enumerable(v) => {
                println!("enum {}::{}", v.definition().name(), v.variant().name());
                v.visit(self);
            }
            Value::Listable(v) => {
                println!("list");
                v.visit(self);
            }
            Value::Mappable(v) => {
                println!("map");
                v.visit(self);
            }
            _ => {
                println!("value {:?}", value);
            }
        }
    }
    fn visit_named_fields(&mut self, named_fields: &NamedValues<'_>) {
        for (field, value) in named_fields.iter() {
            println!("named field {}", field.name());
            value.visit(self);
        }
    }
    fn visit_unnamed_fields(&mut self, values: &[Value<'_>]) {
        for value in values {
            value.visit(self);
        }
    }
    fn visit_entry(&mut self, key: Value<'_>, value: Value<'_>) {
        println!("key / value");
        key.visit(self);
        value.visit(self);
    }
}
```
Then, use the visitor to visit the value.

```
let hello_world = HelloWorld { message: Message::HelloWorld };
hello_world.visit(&mut Print);
```

# Integer in bnum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bnum/latest/bnum/struct.Integer.html

`pub struct Integer<const S: `[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html), const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), const B: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html) = 0, const OM: [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html) = {OverflowMode::DEFAULT as u8}> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

A fixed-size integer type, generic over signedness, bit width, and overflow behaviour.

`Integer` has four const-generic parameters:

- `S`: determines whether the integer behaves as an unsigned integer (- `S = false`), or a signed integer (- `S = true`);
- `N`: specifies how many bytes should be used to store the integer. The bytes are stored in little endian order (least significant byte first).
- `B`: specifies the bit width of the integer. If- `B = 0`(the default value), then the bit width of the integer is taken to be- `N * 8`. Otherwise, the bit width is taken to be- `B`, and in this case it is required that- `N - 8 < B*8 <= N`(i.e.- `N = B.div_ceil(8)`).
- `OM`: specifies the behaviour of the type when arithmetic overflow occurs. There are three valid overflow modes, each corresponding to a variant of the- `OverflowMode`- `0`(- `Wrap`
- `1`(- `Panic`
- `2`(- `Saturate`
 By default,- `OM`is set to- `0`if the- `overflow-checks`flag- `1`if- `overflow-checks`is enabled.

`Integer` closely follows the API and behaviour of Rust’s primitive integer types: `u8`, `i8`, `u16`, `i16`, `u32`, `i32`, `u64`, `i64`, `u128`, `i128`, `usize` and `isize`. The only differences are:

- The primitive integers are stored in native-endian byte order. `Integer`s are always stored in little-endian byte order.
- Primitive integers are serialised in `serde``Integer`s are serialised using`derive(Serialize)`
- In `no-alloc`environments, primitive integers are formatted as decimal strings by the`Debug``Integer`s are formatted as padded hexadecimal strings.
- The primitive integers panic on arithmetic overflow if `overflow-checks``overflow-checks`is disabled. The overflow behaviour of`Integer`is determined by`Self::OVERFLOW_MODE`- `Wrap`- `Wrapping(T)`- `overflow-checks`is disabled).
- `Panic`- `overflow-checks`is enabled.
- `Saturate`- `Saturating(T)`
- `OverflowMode::DEFAULT`

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/consts.rs.html#28-36)

#### pub const [OVERFLOW_MODE](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.OVERFLOW_MODE): [OverflowMode](https://docs.rs/enum.OverflowMode.html)

The overflow mode used for this type, determined by the const-generic parameter `OM`:

- If `OM`is`0`, the overflow mode is`OverflowMode::Wrap`
- If `OM`is`1`, the overflow mode is`OverflowMode::Panic`
- If `OM`is`2`, the overflow mode is`OverflowMode::Saturate`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
use bnum::OverflowMode;

type U264w = t!(U264w);
type I155p = t!(I155p);
type I512s = t!(I512s);

assert_eq!(U264w::OVERFLOW_MODE, OverflowMode::Wrap);
assert_eq!(I155p::OVERFLOW_MODE, OverflowMode::Panic);
assert_eq!(I512s::OVERFLOW_MODE, OverflowMode::Saturate);
```
The minimum value that this type can represent. For unsigned integers, this is `0`. For signed integers, this is `-2^(Self::BITS - 1)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```

use bnum::types::{U512, I512};

assert_eq!(U512::MIN, n!(0));
assert_eq!(I512::MIN.trailing_zeros(), 511); // memory representation is 100...0
```
The maximum value that this type can represent. For unsigned integers, this is `2^Self::BITS - 1`. For signed integers, this is `2^(Self::BITS - 1) - 1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```

assert_eq!(U256::MAX.not(), U256::MIN); // memory representation of `Self::MAX` is 111...1
assert_eq!(I256::MAX.not(), I256::MIN); // memory representation of `Self::MAX` is 011...1
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/bigint_helpers.rs.html#29-37)#### pub const fn [carrying_add](https://docs.rs#method.carrying_add)(self, rhs: Self, carry: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> (Self, [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/bigint_helpers.rs.html#29-37)

#### pub const fn [carrying_add](https://docs.rs#method.carrying_add)(self, rhs: Self, carry: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> (Self, [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Computes `self + rhs + carry`, and returns a tuple of the low (wrapping) bits and the high (carry) bit of the result, in that order.

If `carry` is false, then this method is equivalent to [ overflowing_add](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.overflowing_add).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
use bnum::types::{U1024, I1024};
assert_eq!(n!(1U1024).carrying_add(n!(1), true), (n!(3), false));
assert_eq!(U1024::MAX.carrying_add(n!(1), false), (n!(0), true));
assert_eq!(U1024::MAX.carrying_add(U1024::MAX, true), (U1024::MAX, true));
assert_eq!(n!(1I1024).carrying_add(n!(1), true), (n!(3), false));
assert_eq!(I1024::MAX.carrying_add(n!(0), true), (I1024::MIN, true));
assert_eq!(I1024::MAX.carrying_add(I1024::MAX, true), (n!(-1), true));
assert_eq!(I1024::MIN.carrying_add(I1024::MIN, true), (n!(1), true));
```

```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/bits.rs.html#285-295)#### pub const fn [unbounded_shr](https://docs.rs#method.unbounded_shr)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/bits.rs.html#285-295)

#### pub const fn [unbounded_shr](https://docs.rs#method.unbounded_shr)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> Self

Right-shifts `self` by `rhs` bits. If `rhs` is larger than or equal to `Self::BITS`, then the entire value is shifted out, and:

- for unsigned integers, `0`is returned.
- for signed integers, `-1`is returned if`self`is negative, and`0`is returned if`self`is non-negative.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-19)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
use bnum::types::{U1024, I1024};
assert_eq!(n!(2U1024).unbounded_shr(1), n!(1));
assert_eq!(U1024::MAX.unbounded_shr(1024), n!(0));
assert_eq!(U1024::MAX.unbounded_shr(1030), n!(0));
assert_eq!(I1024::MIN.unbounded_shr(1023), n!(-1));
assert_eq!(n!(-1I1024).unbounded_shr(1024), n!(-1));
assert_eq!(I1024::MAX.unbounded_shr(1025), n!(0));
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/bits.rs.html#317-325)#### pub const fn [reverse_bits](https://docs.rs#method.reverse_bits)(self) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/bits.rs.html#317-325)

#### pub const fn [reverse_bits](https://docs.rs#method.reverse_bits)(self) -> Self

Reverses the order of the bits of `self`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-20)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
type U24 = Uint<3>;
type I24 = Int<3>;
let a: U24 = 0b10110011_11001010_00011101.as_();
assert_eq!(a.reverse_bits(), 0b10111000_01010011_11001101.as_());
let b: I24 = 0b01101001_00111100_11100011.as_();
assert_eq!(b.reverse_bits(), 0b11000111_00111100_10010110.as_());
```
Returns a boolean representing the bit in the given position (`true` if the bit is 1). The least significant bit is at index `0`, the most significant bit is at index `Self::BITS - 1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-21)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
let a = n!(0b1101001101U24);
for i in [0, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9] {
    assert!(a.bit(i));
}
let b = n!(0b0010110010I24);
for i in [1, 4, 5, 7] {
    assert!(b.bit(i));
}
```
Sets/unsets the bit in the given position (i.e. to `1` if `value` is `true`). The least significant bit is at index `0`, the most significant bit is at index `Self::BITS - 1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-22)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
let mut a = n!(0b1001011001001U24);
a.set_bit(2, true);
assert_eq!(a, n!(0b1001011001101));
a.set_bit(1, false); // no change
assert_eq!(a, n!(0b1001011001101));
let mut b = n!(0b010010110110100I24);
b.set_bit(4, false);
assert_eq!(b, n!(0b010010110100100));
b.set_bit(0, false); // no change
assert_eq!(b, n!(0b010010110100100));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/bytes.rs.html#116-122)#### pub const fn [from_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.from_bytes)(digits: [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html); [N](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)]) -> Self

#### pub const fn [from_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.from_bytes)(digits: [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html); [N](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)]) -> Self

Creates a new integer from the given array of bytes. The first byte in the array is interpreted as the least significant byte, the last byte in the array is interpreted as the most significant byte.

If [ Self::BITS](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#associatedconstant.BITS) is not a multiple of

`8`, then the high-order bits are ignored.This method is equivalent to [ from_le_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.from_le_bytes).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-28)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bnum::prelude::*;

type U24 = Uint<3>;
type I24 = Int<3>;
type U15 = t!(U15);

let bytes = [0x56, 0x34, 0x12];
assert_eq!(U24::from_bytes(bytes), n!(0x123456));

let bytes = [0xFE, 0xDC, 0x7B];
assert_eq!(I24::from_bytes(bytes), n!(0x7BDCFE));

assert_eq!(U15::from_bytes([0xFF, 0xFF]), U15::MAX); // = 0x7FFF. the high-order bit is ignored
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/bytes.rs.html#164-202)#### pub const fn [from_be_slice](https://docs.rs#method.from_be_slice)(slice: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>

#### pub const fn [from_be_slice](https://docs.rs#method.from_be_slice)(slice: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>

Converts the slice of big endian bytes to an integer. An empty slice is interpreted as zero. If the value represented by the bytes is too large to be stored in `Self`, then `None` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-29)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;

type U24 = Uint<3>;
type I24 = Int<3>;

assert_eq!(c, Some(a));
let d = U24::from_be_slice(&[0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x5C, 0xF1]);
assert_eq!(d, Some(a));

let e = U24::from_be_slice(&[0x01, 0x00, 0x5C, 0xF1]);
assert_eq!(e, None);

let a: I24 = n!(0xFF8A06).cast_signed();
assert!(a.is_negative());

let b = I24::from_be_slice(&[0xFF, 0x8A, 0x06]);
assert_eq!(b, Some(a));

let c = I24::from_be_slice(&[0xFF, 0xFF, 0x8A, 0x06]);
assert_eq!(c, Some(a));

let d = I24::from_be_slice(&[0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0x8A, 0x06]);
assert_eq!(d, Some(a));

let e = I24::from_be_slice(&[0xFE, 0xFF, 0x8A, 0x06]);
assert_eq!(e, None);
```

#### pub const fn [checked_next_multiple_of](https://docs.rs#method.checked_next_multiple_of)(self, rhs: Self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>

If `rhs` is positive, computes the smallest integer multiple of `rhs` that is greater than or equal to `self`. If `rhs` is negative, computes the largest integer multiple of `rhs` that is less than or equal to `self`.

Returns `None` if `rhs` is zero, or if the result is too large or too small to be represented by `Self`.

assert_eq!(n!(17U256).checked_next_multiple_of(n!(7)), Some(n!(21)));
assert_eq!(n!(1U256).checked_next_multiple_of(n!(0)), None);
assert_eq!(U256::MAX.checked_next_multiple_of(n!(2)), None);
assert_eq!(U256::MAX.checked_next_multiple_of(n!(1)), Some(U256::MAX));

assert_eq!(n!(-9I256).checked_next_multiple_of(n!(-3)), Some(n!(-9)));
assert_eq!(n!(-10I256).checked_next_multiple_of(n!(4)), Some(n!(-8)));
assert_eq!(n!(-17I256).checked_next_multiple_of(n!(-4)), Some(n!(-20)));
assert_eq!(n!(83I256).checked_next_multiple_of(n!(-6)), Some(n!(78)));
assert_eq!(I256::MIN.checked_next_multiple_of(n!(2)), Some(I256::MIN));
assert_eq!(n!(0I256).checked_next_multiple_of(n!(3)), Some(n!(0)));
```

```

#### pub const fn [rem_euclid](https://docs.rs#method.rem_euclid)(self, rhs: Self) -> Self

Returns the [Euclidean remainder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_division) of `self` by `rhs`. This is always equivalent to `self.strict_rem_euclid(rhs)`, regardless of `Self::OVERFLOW_MODE`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-59)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(n!(37U1024).rem_euclid(n!(8)), n!(5));
assert_eq!(n!(-37I1024).rem_euclid(n!(-8)), n!(3));
```
Computes the arithmetic mean of `self` and `rhs`, rounded towards zero (i.e. `(self + rhs) / 2`), without the possibility of overflow.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-61)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(n!(10U256).midpoint(n!(22)), n!(16));
assert_eq!(n!(12U256).midpoint(n!(21)), n!(16));
assert_eq!(n!(-10I256).midpoint(n!(2)), n!(-4));
assert_eq!(n!(-13I256).midpoint(n!(0)), n!(-6));
```
Computes logarithm of `self` to the given `base`, rounded down, i.e. the largest integer `n` such that `base^n <= self`.

Note that you should use `ilog2` or `ilog10` for base-2 or base-10 logarithms respectively, as these are more efficient.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-2)Panics

This function will panic if `self` is less than or equal to zero, or if `base` is less than 2.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-64)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(n!(243U1024).ilog(n!(3)), 5);
assert_eq!(n!(124I1024).ilog(n!(5)), 2);
```
Computes the absolute difference between `self` and `other`, i.e. `|self - other|`, without the possibility of overflow.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-65)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(n!(12U2048).abs_diff(n!(30)), n!(18));
assert_eq!(n!(-12I2048).abs_diff(n!(5)), n!(17));
```

#### pub const fn [next_multiple_of](https://docs.rs#method.next_multiple_of)(self, rhs: Self) -> Self

If `rhs` is positive, computes the smallest integer multiple of `rhs` that is greater than or equal to `self`. If `rhs` is negative, computes the largest integer multiple of `rhs` that is less than or equal to `self`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-3)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

This function will also panic if overflow occurs and [ Self::OVERFLOW_MODE](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#associatedconstant.OVERFLOW_MODE) is

[.](https://docs.rs/enum.OverflowMode.html#variant.Panic)

assert_eq!(n!(-17I256).next_multiple_of(n!(-11)), n!(-22));
```

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-86)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
use bnum::types::{U512, I512};
assert_eq!(n!(13U512).overflowing_rem_euclid(n!(5)), (n!(3), false));
assert_eq!(n!(-23I512).overflowing_rem_euclid(n!(4)), (n!(1), false));
assert_eq!(I512::MIN.overflowing_rem_euclid(n!(-1)), (n!(0), true));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/radix/from_radix.rs.html#234-246)#### pub const fn [from_radix_be](https://docs.rs#method.from_radix_be)(buf: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)], radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/radix/from_radix.rs.html#234-246)

#### pub const fn [from_radix_be](https://docs.rs#method.from_radix_be)(buf: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)], radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>

Converts a slice of big-endian digits in the given radix to an integer. Each `u8` of the slice is interpreted as one digit of base `radix` of the number, so this function will return `None` if any digit is greater than or equal to `radix`, or if the integer represented by the digits is too large to be represented by `Self`. Otherwise, the integer is wrapped in `Some`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-12)Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 256 inclusive.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-96)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
use bnum::types::U512;
let a = U512::from_radix_be(&[4, 3, 2, 1], 11).unwrap();
let b: U512 = n!(1)*n!(11).pow(0) + n!(2)*n!(11).pow(1) + n!(3)*n!(11).pow(2) + n!(4)*n!(11).pow(3);
assert_eq!(a, b); // 4*11^3 + 3*11^2 + 2*11^1 + 1*11^0
```

Converts a string slice in a given base to an integer.

The string is expected to be an optional `+` (or `-` if the integer is signed) sign followed by digits. Leading and trailing whitespace represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals) also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:

- `a-z`
- `A-Z`

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36 inclusive.

let digits = &[1, 67, 88, 200, 55, 68, 87, 120, 178];
let n = U512::from_radix_le(digits, 250).unwrap();

```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/radix/to_radix.rs.html#362-376)#### pub fn [to_str_radix](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_radix)(&self, radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

**crate feature **`alloc` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bnum/integer/radix/to_radix.rs.html#362-376)

#### pub fn [to_str_radix](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_radix)(&self, radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

**crate feature**only.

`alloc`Returns the integer as a string in the given radix.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-18)Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36 inclusive.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-101)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
use bnum::types::{U512, I512};
let src = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz";
let n = U512::from_str_radix(src, 36).unwrap();
assert_eq!(n.to_str_radix(36), src);

let a: I512 = n!(-0o123456701234567);
assert_eq!(a.to_str_radix(8), "-123456701234567");
```

#### pub const fn [saturating_add](https://docs.rs#method.saturating_add)(self, rhs: Self) -> Self

Saturating integer addition. Computes `self + rhs`, returning `Self::MAX` if the result is too large to be represented by `Self`, or `Self::MIN` if the result is too small to be represented by `Self`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-102)Examples

Basic usage:

```

assert_eq!(U1024::MAX.saturating_add(U1024::MAX), U1024::MAX);

assert_eq!(I1024::MIN.saturating_add(n!(-1)), I1024::MIN);
assert_eq!(I1024::MAX.saturating_add(n!(1)), I1024::MAX);
```

For unsigned integers, overflow will occur unless `self` is `0`. For signed integers, overflow will only occur if `self` is [ Self::MIN](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#associatedconstant.MIN).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-121)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;

assert_eq!(n!(0U24).strict_neg(), n!(0));
assert_eq!(n!(5I24).strict_neg(), n!(-5));
```
The following examples will panic due to overflow:

#### pub const fn [wrapping_add](https://docs.rs#method.wrapping_add)(self, rhs: Self) -> Self

Wrap integer addition. Computes `self + rhs` modulo `Self::MAX + 1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-130)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
use bnum::types::{U1024, I1024};

assert_eq!(n!(1U1024).wrapping_add(n!(1)), n!(2));
assert_eq!(U1024::MAX.wrapping_add(n!(1)), n!(0));

assert_eq!(I1024::MIN.wrapping_add(n!(-1)), I1024::MAX);
assert_eq!(I1024::MAX.wrapping_add(n!(1)), I1024::MIN);
```

assert_eq!(n!(0U1024).wrapping_neg(), n!(0));

assert_eq!(n!(1I1024).wrapping_neg(), n!(-1));
assert_eq!(I1024::MIN.wrapping_neg(), I1024::MIN);
```

Panic-free left shift. Returns `self << (rhs % Self::BITS)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-138)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
use bnum::types::{U2048, I2048};

assert_eq!(n!(1U2048).wrapping_shl(1), n!(2));
assert_eq!(n!(1U2048).wrapping_shl(2049), n!(2));

assert_eq!(n!(-2I2048).wrapping_shl(1), n!(-4));
assert_eq!(n!(-2I2048).wrapping_shl(2049), n!(-4));
assert_eq!(n!(-2I2048).wrapping_shl(2048), n!(-2));
```

# bnum::types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bnum/latest/bnum/types/index.html

## Expand description

Type aliases for unsigned and signed integers.

Each type alias has the same overflow behaviour as that of the primitive integer types, i.e. wrap on overflow if `overflow-checks` are disabled and panic on overflow if `overflow-checks` are enabled.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [I128](https://docs.rs/type.I128.html)
- 128-bit signed integer type.
- [I256](https://docs.rs/type.I256.html)
- 256-bit signed integer type.
- [I512](https://docs.rs/type.I512.html)
- 512-bit signed integer type.
- [I1024](https://docs.rs/type.I1024.html)
- 1024-bit signed integer type.
- [I2048](https://docs.rs/type.I2048.html)
- 2048-bit signed integer type.
- [I4096](https://docs.rs/type.I4096.html)
- 4096-bit signed integer type.
- [I8192](https://docs.rs/type.I8192.html)
- 8192-bit signed integer type.
- [U128](https://docs.rs/type.U128.html)
- 128-bit unsigned integer type.
- [U256](https://docs.rs/type.U256.html)
- 256-bit unsigned integer type.
- [U512](https://docs.rs/type.U512.html)
- 512-bit unsigned integer type.
- [U1024](https://docs.rs/type.U1024.html)
- 1024-bit unsigned integer type.
- [U2048](https://docs.rs/type.U2048.html)
- 2048-bit unsigned integer type.
- [U4096](https://docs.rs/type.U4096.html)
- 4096-bit unsigned integer type.
- [U8192](https://docs.rs/type.U8192.html)
- 8192-bit unsigned integer type.

# n in bnum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bnum/latest/bnum/macro.n.html

```
macro_rules! n {
    ($literal_str: literal) => { ... };
    ($ty: ident) => { ... };
    ($($_: tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Create constant [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) values from native integer literals.

`n!` converts integer literals to [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) values at compile time. It supports literals in base 2, 8, 10 and 16:

- The prefix `0b`indicates a binary literal (base 2).
- The prefix `0o`indicates an octal literal (base 8).
- The prefix `0x`indicates a hexadecimal literal (base 16).
- Literals are treated as decimal literals (base 10) if no prefix is specified.

`n!` accepts two forms of integer literal as input:

- Suffix-free, e.g. `n!(0xABCDEF)`. In this case, the const-generic parameters of the created`Integer``let a: Integer<false, 16> = n!(0xABCDEF);`would be valid, but`let b = n!(0xABCDEF);`would trigger a compile error (unless`b`was subsequently used in a context which allowed for type inference).
- With a suffix, e.g. `n!(0xabcdefU128w)`. The suffix may be any valid argument to the`t!`*type descriptor*, as it specifies the values of the const-generic parameters of the created`Integer``t!`

Invoking `n!` with invalid arguments will also trigger a compile error. This can happen if:

- The literal is out of range for the target type (works for inferred types and types specified by a suffix). Note that this will always cause a compile error, regardless of the overflow mode of the type.
- The literal contains an invalid digit.
- A `-`sign appears at the start of the literal when the type is unsigned, e.g.`n!(-123U256)`.
- The suffix is an invalid type descriptor.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*; // n! and t! are re-exported in the prelude

let a: t!(U256) = n!(0xABCDEF); // type inferred from context
```
```
use bnum::prelude::*;

let b = n!(123456_I511s); // type specified by the suffix
// suffix specifies signed 511-bit integer with saturating overflow behaviour
// note that we don't need to define a type alias I511s here
```
The following example will fail to compile, since the compiler is unable to infer the type of the integer:

The following example will fail to compile, since the literal is out of range for the specified type:

The following example will fail to compile, since the literal contains an invalid digit for the specified base:

The following example will fail to compile, since the given type descriptor is invalid:

# t in bnum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bnum/latest/bnum/macro.t.html

```
macro_rules! t {
    ($ty: ident) => { ... };
    ($($_: tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Returns a concrete instantiation of the [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) type with the specified const-generic parameters from a type descriptor.

`t!` takes a type descriptor (which is an identifier fragment) and simply outputs [ Integer<S, N, B, OM>](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html), where the values of the const-generic parameters

`S`, `N`, `B` and `OM` are determined from the type descriptor.A type descriptor has the following format: `<sign><bit_width><overflow_mode>?`:

-
`<sign>`is either`I`(specifying a signed integer) or`U`(specifying an unsigned integer).
-
`<bit_width>`is a decimal integer specifying the bit width of the integer type. The bit width must be at least`2`and at most`2^32 - 1`.
-
`<overflow_mode>`is optional, and if specified must be one of:- `w`for wrapping overflow mode (- `OverflowMode::Wrap`
- `p`for panicking overflow mode (- `OverflowMode::Panic`
- `s`for saturating overflow mode (- `OverflowMode::Saturate`
 If `<overflow_mode>`is omitted, the default overflow mode (`OverflowMode::DEFAULT`

If the given type descriptor is not in this format, a compile error will be triggered when the type is used (when the type is unused, no compile-error will be triggered).

If you want to create [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) values rather than types, use the

[macro.](https://docs.rs/macro.n.html)

`n!`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;

type MyInt = t!(I259p); // signed 259-bit integer with panicking overflow mode
type MyUint = t!(U633); // unsigned 633-bit integer with default overflow mode
type MyInt2 = t!(I538s); // signed 538-bit integer with saturating overflow mode
type MyUint2 = t!(U24w); // unsigned 24-bit integer with wrapping overflow mode
```
The following examples will fail to compile, since the type descriptor is invalid. Note the type must be used in order to trigger the compile error.

## Expand description

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

Specifies that arithmetic operations should wrap around on overflow.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Panic)

### Panic = 1

Specifies that arithmetic operations should panic on overflow.

Specifies that arithmetic operations should saturate to the integer type’s maximum or minimum value on overflow.

# Int in bnum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bnum/latest/bnum/type.Int.html

`pub type Int<const N: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), const B: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html) = 0, const OM: [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html) = {OverflowMode::DEFAULT as u8}> = [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)<true, N, B, OM>;## Expand description

Signed integer type with const-generic bit width and overflow behaviour.

By default, the overflow behaviour is the same as the primitive integer types (i.e. panicking when the `overflow-checks` flag is enabled, and wrapping when `overflow-checks` is disabled).

For more details on how the const-generic parameters are interpreted, see the documentation for [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

# Uint in bnum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bnum/latest/bnum/type.Uint.html

`pub type Uint<const N: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), const B: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html) = 0, const OM: [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html) = {OverflowMode::DEFAULT as u8}> = [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)<false, N, B, OM>;## Expand description

Unsigned integer type with const-generic bit width and overflow behaviour.

By default, the overflow behaviour is the same as the primitive integer types (i.e. panicking when the `overflow-checks` flag is enabled, and wrapping when `overflow-checks` is disabled).

For more details on how the const-generic parameters are interpreted, see the documentation for [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

## Aliased Type[§](https://docs.rs#aliased-type)

Each `u8` of the slice is interpreted as one digit of base `radix` of the number, so this function will return `None` if any digit is greater than or equal to `radix`, or if the integer represented by the digits is too large to be represented by `Self`. Otherwise, the integer is wrapped in `Some`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-2)Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 256 inclusive.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
use bnum::prelude::*;
use bnum::types::U512;
let a = U512::from_radix_be(&[4, 3, 2, 1], 11).unwrap();
let b: U512 = n!(1)*n!(11).pow(0) + n!(2)*n!(11).pow(1) + n!(3)*n!(11).pow(2) + n!(4)*n!(11).pow(3);
assert_eq!(a, b); // 4*11^3 + 3*11^2 + 2*11^1 + 1*11^0
```

# sim_lib_skill - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-skill/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_skill/

## Expand description

Agent skills for the SIM runtime.

A *skill* is a callable capability that an agent can invoke – a tool, a
model, a resource, a prompt, a memory, a retriever, a judge, or a router.
Each skill is described by a [ SkillCard](https://docs.rs/struct.SkillCard.html) that pairs a stable identity and
symbol with input and output

[contracts, a](https://docs.rs/sim-shape/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_shape/index.html)

`sim_shape`[governing caching/recording/privacy, and the transport that actually runs the call. Cards are bound into a](https://docs.rs/struct.SkillPolicy.html)

`SkillPolicy`[and exposed as ordinary callable runtime objects through](https://docs.rs/struct.SkillRegistry.html)

`SkillRegistry`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.SkillCallable.html)

`SkillCallable`Behavior is provided by a [ SkillTransport](https://docs.rs/trait.SkillTransport.html): a backend (fixture, HTTP, MCP,
process, OpenAI-compatible server, …) that knows how to discover and call
skills.

[registers the](https://docs.rs/struct.SkillLib.html)

`SkillLib``skill/*` operations (install, bind,
list, card, call, and the feature-gated audit/tool/runner/serve surfaces)
when the library is loaded into a [.](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/env/core/struct.Cx.html)

`sim_kernel::Cx`Optional Cargo features select transports and integrations: `mcp`, `http`,
`openai`, `process`, `agent`, `runner`, `serve`, and the `cache`/`cassette`
recording surfaces.

# noslop - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/noslop/0.2.0/noslop/

## Expand description

noslop - Pre-commit checks with acknowledgment tracking

This library provides the core functionality for:

- Defining checks that must be reviewed when code changes
- Tracking acknowledgments that prove review happened
- Integrating with git hooks for enforcement

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

The library follows a hexagonal (ports & adapters) architecture:

-
`core`- `core::models`
- `core::ports`
- `core::services`

-
`adapters`- `adapters::toml`
- `adapters::git`
- `adapters::trailer`
- `adapters::file`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use noslop::core::models::{Check, Acknowledgment, Severity};
use noslop::adapters::TomlCheckRepository;
use noslop::core::ports::CheckRepository;
// Create a repository for checks
let repo = TomlCheckRepository::current_dir()?;
// Find checks for changed files
let checks = repo.find_for_files(&["src/main.rs".to_string()])?;
```

# cumulus_client_pov_recovery - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cumulus-client-pov-recovery/0.32.0/cumulus_client_pov_recovery/

## Expand description

Parachain PoV recovery

A parachain needs to build PoVs that are send to the relay chain to progress. These PoVs are erasure encoded and one piece of it is stored by each relay chain validator. As the relay chain decides on which PoV per parachain to include and thus, to progress the parachain it can happen that the block corresponding to this PoV isn’t propagated in the parachain network. This can have several reasons, either a malicious collator that managed to include its own PoV and doesn’t want to share it with the rest of the network or maybe a collator went down before it could distribute the block in the network. When something like this happens we can use the PoV recovery algorithm implemented in this crate to recover a PoV and to propagate it with the rest of the network.

It works in the following way:

-
For every included relay chain block we note the backed candidate of our parachain. If the block belonging to the PoV is already known, we do nothing. Otherwise we start a timer that waits for a randomized time inside a specified interval before starting to recover the PoV.
-
If between starting and firing the timer the block is imported, we skip the recovery of the PoV.
-
If the timer fired we recover the PoV using the relay chain PoV recovery protocol.

4a. After it is recovered, we restore the block and import it.

4b. Since we are trying to recover pending candidates, availability is not guaranteed. If the block PoV is not yet available, we retry.

If we need to recover multiple PoV blocks (which should hopefully not happen in real life), we make sure that the blocks are imported in the correct order.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [PoVRecovery](https://docs.rs/struct.PoVRecovery.html)
- Encapsulates the logic of the pov recovery.
- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/struct.RecoveryDelayRange.html)- Delay - Range
- The delay between observing an unknown block and triggering the recovery of a block. Randomizing the start of the recovery within this interval can be used to prevent self-DOSing if the recovery request is part of a distributed protocol and there is the possibility that multiple actors are requiring to perform the recovery action at approximately the same time.
- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/struct.RecoveryRequest.html)- Request
- Structure used to trigger an explicit recovery request via `PoVRecovery`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/enum.RecoveryKind.html)- Kind
- Type of recovery to trigger.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/trait.RecoveryHandle.html)- Handle
- Test-friendly wrapper trait for the overseer handle. Can be used to simulate failing recovery requests.

# snowbridge_pallet_inbound_queue_v2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/snowbridge-pallet-inbound-queue-v2/0.14.0/snowbridge_pallet_inbound_queue_v2/

## Expand description

Inbound Queue

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

Receives messages emitted by the Gateway contract on Ethereum, whereupon they are verified, translated to XCM, and finally sent to AssetHub for further processing.

Message relayers are rewarded in wrapped Ether that is included within the message. This wrapped Ether is derived from Ether that the message origin has locked up on Ethereum.

# aegis-id 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/aegis-id/0.1.0

# Aegis ID

Aegis ID is a terminal password-rule puzzle disguised as a very ordinary account enrollment console.

The program asks for a username and password, then quietly adds increasingly restrictive password requirements. Failed attempts only show the requirements that are currently not satisfied. Once every rule is satisfied, the console clears and asks you to rewrite the password exactly.
